claims.text: Integrating high-throughput first-principles simulations with machine learning can reliably identify refractory high-entropy alloy compositions.
The identified RHEA compositions can simultaneously exhibit high strength, ductility, and low density.
Optimizing composition to favor solid-solution strengthening and phase stability produces the desired combination of properties.
The relevant starting RHEA systems contain multiple principal elements in a random solid solution.
A combined simulation and machine-learning workflow can screen and refine RHEA composition space.
DFT calculations and experimental datasets can be used as inputs for training the machine-learning model.
Predicted phase stability mediates the mechanical properties of the designed alloys.
Solid-solution homogeneity and alloy microstructure mediate the mechanical properties of the designed alloys.
Physics-informed machine learning can guide high-throughput first-principles simulations to correlate alloy composition with thermomechanical behavior.
The workflow can identify compositions whose atomic interactions favor solid-solution strengthening.
The workflow can identify compositions whose atomic interactions favor ductile deformation mechanisms.
The workflow can limit alloy density through composition selection.
The approach will yield RHEA compositions with greater yield strength than compositions produced by conventional trial-and-error methods or existing compositions in similar alloy families.
The approach will yield RHEA compositions with greater ductility than compositions produced by conventional trial-and-error methods or existing compositions in similar alloy families.
Conventional empirical or limited thermokinetic design approaches do not explore the full RHEA compositional space at high resolution.
Model predictions may be less accurate when intermetallic or other secondary phases dominate.
Model predictions may be less accurate when extrapolating beyond the training-data range.
